newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Taleban threaten cultural relics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taleban threaten cultural relics.

text.p: A threat by a commander of the purist Islamic Taleban in Afghanistan to dynamite two monumental, 1,500-year-old statues of the Buddha has sparked fresh concern for the country's cultural heritage.
Commander Ahmadzai, whose forces are trying to take the Bamiyan area where the sculptures stand, told journalists last week: "We will destroy them because Islam has forbidden statues."
Taleban authorities in Kabul say the commander has no authority to make such a threat.

The threat prompted United Nations secretary-general Kofi Annan to appeal on Thursday to political and military commanders in Afghanistan to ensure that no harm comes to the scuptures. India and Sri Lanka have also expressed concern.
Afghanistan has been a cross-roads of cultures and religions for thousands of years and each has left its mark.

But even Ghenghis Khan, possibly the greatest vandal of all time, whose troops rampaged through Asia seven hundred years ago levelling some of the greatest civilisations of the period, was unable to do as much damage to Afghanistan's history and heritage as the last 20 years of war in the country.

Greek cities founded by Alexander the Great that had lain undisturbed for centuries, apart from the delicate attentions of archaeologists' trowels, are now being flattened to improve access for treasure hunters.
BULLDOZERS

"Ai Khanum (the site of a major Alexandrine city in northern Afghanistan) has been raked flat with bulldozers and tractors to facilitate individual diggers with their shovels and pick axes." says a report from the Society for the Preservation of Afghanistan's Cultural Heritage (SPACH).
The report says that previously unknown sites are also being destroyed.

"Many hitherto unknown sites have come to light, unearthed in the course of the fighting and destruction by rockets and bombing. These also are being systematically destroyed by the local population incited by the prospect of finding gold." according to SPACH.
Other parts of Afghanistan's heritage, 1,700-year-old buddhist shrines at Hadda in the east of the country -- are also being destroyed, but for more mundane reasons.
"Trucks are removing stones from Hadda -- to be used as building materials," says the SPACH report.
MUSEUM A SHATTERED SHELL

Kabul's museum is a shattered shell: less than 30 percent of its world-class collection survived the looting after Kabul fell to the mujahedin in 1992. The remains of the collection, many pieces broken beyond repair, languish behind steel doors in makeshift store rooms built in the restaurant of a Kabul hotel.

The two huge 4th century Buddhas of Bamiyan, one 38 metres (125 feet) high and the other 55 metres (180 feet) high -- the tallest standing Buddha in the world -- were carved out of a sandstone cliff in central Afghanistan when Europe was deep in the dark ages.

They had not escaped damage in the intervening centuries: when Islam first arrived in Afghanistan their faces were destroyed. Despite this indignity, and being used more recently for target practice by young men armed with rocket-propelled grenades and Kalashnikovs, the two colossi have maintained their serene watch over the verdant pastures of the Bamiyan valley.

For the moment the statues are in the control of one of the factions that make up the anti-Taleban alliance. The Taleban have sworn to dislodge the opposition, take the rest of Afghanistan, and create a pure Islamic state in the country.
In the strict view of the Taleban, the depiction of living beings is against Islamic law.
TALEBAN SAY COMMANDER HAS NO AUTHORITY

The Taleban authorities say that Commander Ahmadzai has no authority to destroy the statues and that no decision has been taken about the future of the Buddhas. They say the question will be referred to the Supreme Court.

"No decision has been made regarding the Buddhas. We preserve all sorts of historical relics, from all eras, as long as there is no contradiction between Islam and what we have inherited from the past. It will be the job of the Supreme Court to make a decision on this," said the Taleban's acting Minister of information and Culture, Amir Khan Mutaqi, recently.

In the areas they control, the Taleban have generally protected archaeological sites and relics better than other Afghan factions by punishing looters and enforcing stricter controls on the export of antiques.

However, until the fate of representational relics of Afghanistan's pre-Islamic civilisations has been decided, the Taleban's credentials as the guardians of the country's heritage will remain open to question.
